vignette:
Mr. Tran is a quiet man, slight of build, with hands that have known the weight of a welding torch for over forty years. He sits in the chair across from me with his back straight, his eyes fixed on a spot just above my left shoulder. His wife, Linh, urged him to come. “He doesn’t sleep,” she said on the phone. “He wakes up shouting. Sometimes he doesn’t even know where he is.”

He was nineteen in the spring of 1970, living in a small village in central Vietnam. His father was a fisherman; his mother sold vegetables at the morning market. He was apprenticed to a local welder, learning to mend broken plows and bicycle frames. The war felt distant until the morning the sky turned black with smoke from the nearest district. By noon, the soldiers came—not the ones he’d seen on the roads, but men in uniforms he couldn’t identify. They gathered everyone in the square. He remembers the sound of a rooster crowing, then the first shot.

He does not speak of what happened next in detail. He tells me only that he ran. He hid in a drainage ditch for two days, the water up to his chest, the bodies of strangers floating past. He found his parents later, behind the market stall. He buried them himself, with his bare hands.

After the war, he made his way to a refugee camp, then to the United States. He met Linh at a temple in San Jose. They married, had two sons, and he found work in a metal fabrication shop. For years, he welded beams for bridges and railings for schools. He was good at it—steady, precise. The heat of the torch and the smell of molten steel became his constant companions. He told himself the past was sealed, like a weld that had cooled and hardened.

But the past does not cool. It leaks through.

Now, at seventy-four, he still wakes before dawn to go to the shop, though he retired three years ago. He cannot stop. The foreman lets him come in part-time, sweeping, organizing scrap. When he stands at the welding station, even just to watch a younger man work, the hiss of the gas torch takes him back to the ditch—the sounds of shouting, the water’s cold grip. He grips the bench until his knuckles turn white. His hands shake for hours afterward.

Linh says he has not slept through the night in twenty years. He refuses to talk about the war, but his body talks for him. At night, he relives the running, the hiding, the smell of burned rice paddies. He wakes with a jolt, convinced he is back in the village. Once, he mistook a passing helicopter for an attack and dove under the dining table, sending the dishes crashing. His sons were grown by then, but they looked at him with a fear he recognized—the same fear he saw in his own eyes every morning in the cracked mirror above the sink.

He stopped going to the temple because the incense smoke reminded him of the fires. He stopped eating rice because the texture made him think of the mud. He eats only bread now, dry and tasteless, as if to deny his body any comfort it might betray him with.

In our sessions, he speaks slowly, deliberately. He does not use the word “trauma.” He says, “There is a sickness in my sleep.” He tells me about a young man at the shop, a veteran of a different war, who told him that sometimes the past is a landmine you step on years later. Mr. Tran nodded, but his face did not change.

He still goes to the shop. He still holds the torch, even when his hands shake. It is the only place where he feels something close to control—the precision of the flame, the seam of metal fusing, the small act of making something whole. He cannot make himself whole, but he can make a joint hold. He can leave something stronger than he found it.

That is what he tells himself. And then he goes home, sits in the dark, and waits for the first stirring of the night, when the ditch will find him again.
